method: After the record was frozen, the same AI reconstructed the 180 EC from the Arabic Studies table and checked formal progression from the individual course pages. The workbook was rescanned for regional and language coverage, including non-title references. The closest cross-disciplinary palette was re-examined on its actual course contributions before checking the final exception and wording.
findings: The 2026–2027 catalogue identifies the 180 EC Arabic Language and Culture bachelor. The public curriculum gives a 60 EC first year shared by both majors. Arabic Studies then has five taught units of 6 EC, the required Cairo semester of 30 EC, three advanced 6 EC Arabic-source units, 30 EC free choice, and the 12 EC thesis. Middle Eastern Studies follows a distinct regional route after the shared year. The source link formerly targeted the Middle Eastern Studies path; the corrected link is the official catalogue destination labelled Arabic Studies. Dutch is the principal language; Literary Studies of the Modern Middle East is in English, and advanced language and literature work uses Arabic.

Arabic 1 and 2 must be passed before Arabic 3 and 4. Complete the full first year before Year 2, satisfying the first-year Arabic requirement for Arabic Communication and Modern Arabic Literary Discourse, the 48 EC threshold for Literatures of the Modern Middle East and the positive study advice for Philosophy of Science. The reading list continues the literary-discourse unit. Cairo develops Egyptian and Modern Standard Arabic and regional knowledge, before Media Arabic builds on work there. The final thesis requires research with Arabic sources and reports in Dutch or English. Keep the zero-credit Dutch writing diagnostic and recurring tutoring outside the 180 EC. The catalogue distinguishes the first-year diagnostic from the Arabic language sequence.

The strongest combined option starts with the three actual regional or Arabic contacts and adds advanced work in comparative narrative, history, peace studies and media. World Myth & Literature treats Arabic and Near Eastern materials through comparative narrative, while Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean is centred on art and cross-cultural networks and History of Empires uses ancient Persia in a worldwide comparison. This supports a serious comparative humanities topic, but progression across 24 courses would shift toward world literature, global history, or international studies. A regional course cluster cannot sustain the degree’s other central strand even when Arabic-language acquisition is set aside. The workbook has introductory Dutch but no Arabic instruction, and comparative politics, conflict, law and global studies do not form a sustained Middle Eastern or North African sequence. The content gap is established independently of term coverage or scheduling.
